topic: The Fundamental Bridge: The Relationship Between Integrals and Derivatives

sections.title: Prerequisite Warm-up: The Concept of Change
sections.content: Briefly revisit the derivative as 'instantaneous rate of change' (the slope of a tangent line) and the integral as 'accumulation' (the area under a curve). Use a visual analogy of a car's speedometer vs. its odometer.
sections.example: Visualize a robotic turtle moving. The derivative is how fast the turtle moves at a specific tick; the integral is the total path length the turtle has covered over time.

sections.title: The Core Connection: Inverse Operations
sections.content: Explain that differentiation and integration are inverse processes, much like addition and subtraction or multiplication and division. Introduce the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part 1) visually by showing a dynamic rectangle sweeping out an area.
sections.example: Imagine a stack of paper sheets. The derivative tells you the thickness of a single sheet; the integral tells you the total height of the stack.

sections.title: Visual Proof: The Accumulation Function
sections.content: Display an animation of a function f(t). As a vertical line moves across the x-axis, show the area accumulating as a shaded region. Graphically demonstrate how the derivative of this 'area function' maps back to the original function value.
sections.example: A smart-sensor drone monitoring the density of a forest canopy: The accumulation function tracks total biomass as the drone flies forward; the derivative reveals the biomass density at any specific coordinate.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Reinforce the 'Fundamental Bridge' concept: If you differentiate an integral, you return to the starting point. Highlight that this relationship allows us to calculate areas without infinite summation.
sections.example: A recap animation showing a cycle: [Function] -> (Integrate) -> [Area Function] -> (Differentiate) -> [Back to Function]. It’s a closed-loop system!
